newsitem.title: USA: Swiss list continues to produce surprises.
newsitem.headline: Swiss list continues to produce surprises.

text.p: Switzerland's list of unclaimed Holocaust-era bank accounts continued to turn up the names of some dubious depositors on Thursday.

Besides containing the names of hundreds of Holocaust vitctims who sought Swiss banks to safeguard their savings, the list also has been churning up the names of prominent Nazis and collaborators who sought the protection provided by Swiss bank secrecy.

The names of six possible members of Hitler's Nazi elite were discovered when the list was published on Wednesday, and Jewish groups said the names of two more possible major collaborators have now come to light.

The Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Centre said that it appeared that Dr. Vojtech Tuka, listed as living in Vienna, was actually the prime minister of the Nazi puppet government in Slovakia during the war and was responsible for deporting hundreds of Jews to death camps.
The Nazi collaborator was executed in Bratislava in 1946 for war crimes. It was not known how much money was in the unclaimed Tuka account.
Jewish groups said another intriging name on the list was that of Mercier Du Paty, the Marquis De Clam, of Versailles.
Rabbi Abraham Cooper, the associate dean of the Wiesenthal Centre, said Mercier Du Paty might have been the chief of the Vichy government's commission on the Jewish question from March to May 1944.
A previous holder of the Marquis De Clam title was a major opponent of Alfred Dreyfus, the victim in one of Europe's most notorious anti-Semitic chapters, Rabbi Cooper said.
Meanwhile, the Swiss Bankers Association was urgently investigating whether six accounts belonged to prominent Nazis and has asked the Swiss government to help, Cooper said.
The centre faxed the names to the association on Wednesday. Among them was an alias used by an aide to Adolf Eichmann, as well as a close friend of Hitler's and the wife of a Nazi intelligence chief.

One fascist who freely admits he was on the list was Former Spanish Foreign Minister Ramon Serrano Suner, brother-in-law of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco and once a pillar of fascist rule in Spain.
Serrano, 96, and seven members of his family were on the list of unclaimed accounts.
In an interview with Spanish newspapers, Serrano denied he had any dealings in money or property confiscated from Jews by Nazis during the war.
Serrano was a general of the Falangist faction which supported Franco during the Spanish Civil War from 1936-1939. After Franco's victory he was appointed foreign minister, a post he held until 1942.
He was believed to have been influential in persuading Franco to remain neutral during the war instead of aligning Spain with Nazi Germany.
